query: FeNiCrCoCu is considered suitable for thin-film use, and its expense favors applying it as a protective coating on conventional metals rather than using it in bulk. Earlier studies examined room-temperature wear behavior in relation to coating–substrate combinations, composition, and grain size, but largely addressed the alloy itself or a limited thermal regime rather than the overall wear response of a coating across different temperatures. Under the constraints that FeNiCrCoCu remains a thin protective coating and that high-temperature wear is the target application, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its overall wear resistance and why? Specify an intervention relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the observations expected if the hypothesis is correct, state the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, connect the hypothesis to prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Pre-oxidation treatment induces a continuous Cr2O3 and spinel (Fe,Co,Ni,Cu)3O4 layer that acts as a mechanical barrier, significantly reducing the high-temperature wear rate of FeNiCrCoCu thin coatings.
generation.material_initial_state: FeNiCrCoCu thin film coating produced via microwave cladding on SS-304 in the as-deposited state.
generation.intervention: Subject the coating to a pre-oxidation treatment at 800 °C in air for 10 hours.
generation.conditions: High-temperature wear test at 800 °C, under a normal load of 15 N with a sliding distance of 1000 m.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a continuous, adherent oxide scale comprised mainly of Cr2O3 and (Fe,Co,Ni,Cu)3O4.
generation.mechanism: The thermally formed oxide scale provides a physical barrier that reduces direct metal-to-metal contact and limits continued oxidation and mechanical damage under sliding, thereby lowering wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: The pre-oxidized coating exhibits a wear rate approximately 50% lower and a friction coefficient reduced by about 0.2–0.5 relative to the unoxidized baseline.
generation.baseline: As-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating without any pre-oxidation treatment.
generation.boundary: Effective within the temperature range of roughly 700–850 °C and under moderate loads (around 15 N sliding conditions).
generation.uncertainty: Variability in oxide scale uniformity and potential substrate effects may introduce deviations.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu coated samples—one with the 800 °C, 10-hour pre-oxidation treatment and one left as-deposited. Perform identical high-temperature wear tests under a 15 N load and 1000 m sliding distance.
measurements: Oxide scale morphology and continuity via SEM/EDS
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized samples do not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in wear rate or show no improvement in oxide scale continuity compared to the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

R-Sq of Fe and Ni both exceeded 96%, and R-Sq of three elements of Cr, Co and Cu reached almost 80%. Therefore, there is a strong linear correlation between principal element content and tensile strength of FeNiCrCoCu HEA. With increase of the Ni content, tensile strength of HEA increases significantly in Figure 2b–f. Meanwhile, the tensile strength of FeNiCrCoCu HEA also showed an increasing trend as the increasing of Fe and Cr elements. papers.title: Investigation of surface hardness, thermostability, tribo‐corrosion, and microstructural morphological properties of microwave‐synthesized high entrop
papers.approach: Microwave cladding deposition on steel followed by prolonged thermal exposure (~10 weeks at 800 °C) with surface microscopy (SEM, EDS) and wear testing.
papers.findings: After thermal exposure, the coating developed a protective oxide scale consisting of Cr2O3 and (Fe,Co,Ni,Mn,Cu)3O4. This oxide formation was correlated with enhanced corrosion and wear resistance, and modifications in the ferrite grain size were noted.
papers.mechanism: Oxidation of alloying elements during high-temperature exposure forms a continuous protective oxide layer that hinders further oxidation and mechanically shields the substrate, thus reducing wear.

papers.title: Combining Machine Learning and Molecular Dynamics to Predict Mechanical Properties and Microstructural Evolution of FeNiCrCoCu High-Entropy Alloys.
papers.system: FeNiCrCoCu HEA with varied principal element content
papers.approach: Molecular dynamics simulations enhanced by machine learning to correlate individual element content with tensile and compressive mechanical properties along with analysis of microstructural evolution under loading.
papers.findings: A strong linear correlation was observed between the content of elements (especially Ni and Cr) and tensile strength, with non‐monotonic trends for Co and Cu. These results imply that elemental tuning significantly affects the alloy’s mechanical response.
papers.mechanism: Element-specific solid solution strengthening and microstructural evolution (grain morphology and phase distribution) govern the alloy’s mechanical properties, which indirectly impacts wear performance.

papers.title: Microstructure and Corrosive Wear Properties of CoCrFeNiMn High-Entropy Alloy Coatings.
papers.system: CoCrFeNiMn HEA coatings prepared by laser cladding
papers.approach: Laser cladding followed by variable heat-treatment conditions with analyses of phase structure (via SEM and EDS) and testing under corrosive wear environments.
papers.findings: Post heat treatment, oxide scales (involving oxides of Fe, Cr and Mn) formed and were linked to modified wear and corrosion properties. The phase and microstructural evolution of the coating was found to influence the overall wear mechanism.
papers.mechanism: Similar to the FeNiCrCoCu system, heat treatment promotes the formation of protective oxide layers that guard against further oxidation and wear damage.

established: High-temperature exposure leads to the formation of protective oxide scales (e.g., Cr2O3 and spinel oxides) that enhance wear resistance.
Thermal treatments induce significant microstructural changes such as grain growth and phase transformations, which in turn affect mechanical and wear properties.
The elemental composition and ratio in high-entropy alloys strongly influence solid solution strengthening and oxidation behaviour.

approaches_tried.approach: Microwave cladding with extended thermal exposure (~800 °C, up to 10 weeks) in air.
approaches_tried.outcome: Yielded coatings where thermally induced oxide scales (Cr2O3 and spinel) formed, significantly improving wear and corrosive performance.

approaches_tried.approach: Molecular dynamics simulations combined with machine learning to optimize principal element content.
approaches_tried.outcome: Determined correlations between element ratios and tensile strength, highlighting the impact of individual elements; however, direct implications for high-temperature wear remain less explored.

mechanisms: Protective oxide scale formation during high-temperature oxidation, which acts as a barrier reducing further wear.
Microstructural stabilization (grain size and phase distribution) that supports high hardness and wear resistance.
Solid solution strengthening effects stemming from balanced elemental composition.
disagreements: Some studies prioritize composition-dependent mechanical properties (e.g., tensile strength and deformation behaviour) over direct wear performance mechanisms such as oxidation.
There is divergence on the trade-offs in elemental ratios (e.g., excess Co or Cu may improve strength up to a point but may also adversely affect high-temperature stability and oxidation behaviour).
open_questions: Is the dominant factor for overall wear resistance in thin-film FeNiCrCoCu coatings the formation of a protective oxide layer or the intrinsic microstructural features (e.g., grain morphology, phase stability)?
How does the coating–substrate interface influence the durability and effectiveness of the oxide film under varied thermal and loading conditions?
What is the exact interplay between thermal exposure, oxide layer formation, and mechanical damage at high temperatures (beyond room-temperature wear studies)?
opportunities: Investigate targeted thermal treatments or in-situ oxidation control to optimize the protective oxide scale in FeNiCrCoCu thin coatings.
Perform systematic high-temperature wear experiments over a broad range of temperatures and loads to decouple the contributions of oxide layer stability from microstructural effects.
Explore coating–substrate interaction mechanisms, combining thermal cycling with wear testing, to assess the overall performance of FeNiCrCoCu protective coatings in high-temperature applications.

directions.direction: Investigate the role of thermally induced, continuous protective oxide scale formation (e.g., Cr2O3 and spinel (Fe,Co,Ni,Cu)3O4) on high‐temperature wear resistance.
directions.assessment: This direction directly targets the proposed mechanism by examining how controlled oxidation at high temperatures forms a protective scale that reduces wear. The evidence from PMC10908794 supports oxide scale formation in HEA coatings at 800 °C, and this intervention is both feasible and directly relevant to high‐temperature wear.

directions.direction: Examine the impact of microstructural grain refinement on oxide nucleation and stability during high-temperature wear.
directions.assessment: By varying cooling rates during deposition, one can produce fine‐grained versus coarse‐grained coatings. Prior work (PMC10908794 and PMC9960858) shows grain size influences both oxidation and wear behavior; this approach is feasible, though it acts indirectly on the wear mechanism.

directions.direction: Assess the effect of coating–substrate interface engineering via a thin interlayer (e.g., Ni) on the integrity of the protective oxide scale.
directions.assessment: This intervention targets the mechanical and thermal mismatch at the interface, which may lead to spallation of the oxide scale. Improving interfacial bonding is known to support coating integrity. Evidence from thermal stability studies supports the idea that a stable interfacial region enhances coating performance.

directions.direction: Evaluate the benefits of intermittent thermal cycling versus constant high-temperature exposure on the self-healing and densification of the oxide scale.
directions.assessment: Thermal cycling may allow repeated oxidation and healing of microcracks in the oxide layer. Although more complex, this method could stabilize the protective film better than a single, sustained high-temperature exposure. Prior evidence in related HEA system studies suggests that cyclic exposures influence oxide integrity.

directions.direction: Modulate deposition parameters (such as substrate preheating) to influence the initial defect density and thereby affect subsequent oxidation kinetics.
directions.assessment: While this direction could alter the initial microstructural state and oxidation behavior, its link to overall high-temperature wear resistance is less direct compared to the above strategies and may be more challenging to isolate mechanistically.

candidates.hypothesis: A fine-grained FeNiCrCoCu microstructure, achieved by a high-cooling-rate deposition process, promotes uniform oxide nucleation and an adherent oxide film during high-temperature exposure, thereby lowering the wear rate compared to a coarse-grained microstructure.
candidates.intervention: Modulate the deposition cooling rate to achieve a significantly refined (fine-grained) microstructure versus a standard (coarse-grained) microstructure.

candidates.hypothesis: Incorporation of a thin Ni interlayer between the substrate and the FeNiCrCoCu coating enhances the coating-substrate adhesion and promotes the integrity of the protective oxide scale during high-temperature wear, thus reducing overall wear rate.
candidates.intervention: Deposit a 50 nm Ni interlayer on the SS-304 substrate before applying the FeNiCrCoCu coating.

candidates.hypothesis: Intermittent thermal cycling (alternating periods of high temperature and cooling) promotes the self-healing of the oxide scale on FeNiCrCoCu coatings, resulting in a more stable and continuous protective film that significantly reduces high-temperature wear.
candidates.intervention: Apply intermittent thermal cycles consisting of 1-hour exposure at 800 °C followed by cooling to room temperature, repeated to accumulate a total of 10 hours at high temperature, as opposed to a continuous 10-hour exposure.
